1.name: Caden Wilson
1.about: The No. 2 overall recruit in the country arrives at Kansas already sitting atop early NBA draft boards. Wilson’s combination of 6'5" size, advanced shot-making and polished creation gives him the foundation of a potential primary guard. His freshman season will test whether his playmaking, rim pressure and defense can match his scoring pedigree.

2.name: Jaeden Grimes
2.about: Few incoming guards possess the combination of physical tools and two-way potential that Grimes brings to Washington. Ranked as the No. 3 overall recruit, he pairs explosive athleticism and an exceptional 6'9" wingspan with promising perimeter shooting. Developing his lead-guard creation and playmaking will be central to his push for the No. 1 pick.

3.name: Ja'Corey Washington
3.about: Long before arriving at Kentucky, Washington had established himself as the No. 1 recruit in the country, overwhelming opponents with his physicality and explosiveness. His 7'3" wingspan amplifies his impact as a rebounder, finisher and defensive playmaker. The intrigue now centers on how much offensive skill he can add beyond his already dominant interior game.

4.name: Marc-André Marin
4.about: Marin has emerged as the premier international name entering this draft cycle, with scouts drawn to the defensive havoc he can create at 6'9". His 7'2" wingspan, quick reactions and athleticism allow him to generate steals, challenge shots and explode in transition. His offensive development—particularly his jumper and half-court creation—will shape how high he ultimately climbs.

5.name: J'wuan Anderson
5.about: Anderson arrives at Missouri following a legendary high school career built around scoring and offensive dominance. His deep scoring arsenal, tight handle and advanced one-on-one creativity made him one of the most feared offensive players in his class. Now the question is whether that individual brilliance can translate into efficient creation for an entire college offense.

6.name: Rayan Ewane
6.about: Ewane enters the year as a potential major riser, with some scouts believing his combination of size and developing skill could eventually push him much higher than No. 6. The 7-footer can rebound and ignite transition himself, finish fluidly and use his 7'5" wingspan defensively. A breakout against professional competition could quickly elevate his draft stock.

7.name: Trey Magana
7.about: Unlike most of the names near the top of this board, Magana enters the year with a full college season already behind him. His strength, athleticism and touch around the basket give him an effective interior scoring package, while his defensive versatility adds two-way appeal. The swing skill is obvious: significant shooting improvement could dramatically expand his NBA projection.

8.name: Austin Almanza
8.about: Recruited to UCLA directly from Spain, Almanza enters college basketball as one of the more intriguing international freshmen in the class. His 7'4" wingspan, timing and instincts project particularly well around the rim, where he can erase shots and generate second-chance offense. How quickly he adjusts to the college game offensively and physically will be a major early storyline.

9.name: James Chonokolo
9.about: Chonokolo returns to Duke with an opportunity to make the sophomore leap scouts have been anticipating. At 245 pounds with a 7'3" wingspan, he already brings NBA-caliber strength and length, but his developing perimeter jumper separates him from traditional interior bigs. A larger offensive role could establish him as one of the draft’s most skilled frontcourt prospects.

10.name: Troy Reeves Jr.
10.about: A lights-out shooter throughout his high school career, Reeves earned five-star status and finished as a top-12 recruit nationally. His deep range, quick release and constant off-ball movement make him a threat well beyond the arc. The shooting already looks NBA-caliber; developing his creation and defense could determine whether he climbs beyond specialist projections.
